title: POC latency & throughput SLO scoping with DataWave
next_steps: Maya to send benchmark harness + config and RD-POC template by 2025-03-13
Priya to share production p95/p99 traces and QPS profile by 2025-03-14
Schedule redwood-managed benchmark run week of 2025-03-17 (Luis to propose slots)
action_items: Maya Chen | Send benchmark harness and example configs | 2025-03-13
Luis Ortega | Prepare warm/cold cache test plan + scripts | 2025-03-17
Priya Rao | Export 2 weeks of latency traces, annotate high-cost prompts | 2025-03-14
Mark Liu | Confirm security checklist required for Dedicated/Private pilot | 2025-03-18
summary: POC scoping focused on defining latency (TTFT) vs throughput (TPOT) SLOs for DataWave's chat and bulk-embedding workloads. Agreed on measurement plan: synthetic and production-trace-driven benchmarks, warm vs cold cache, p95/p99 targets per workload class, and concrete next steps to run Redwood-managed benchmarks.
topics: Measurement methodology (client vs server timings, warm/cold, sampling)
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — Maya from Redwood, I'll kick us off.
[00:06] Priya Rao: Hi Maya, hi Luis, thanks. We're mostly here to scope the POC — want to make sure our latency obligations are clear.
[00:14] Luis Ortega: Great, quick intros — I'm Luis, infra/benchmarks on Redwood's side. I'll drive the measurement plan.
[00:20] Sarah Bennett: I'm Sarah, Head of AI. Our key ask: keep chat latency under a hard cap for end-user flows and also make sure batch embedding throughput is predictable for nightly jobs.
[00:32] Maya Chen: Perfect. Priya, can you outline the most common request patterns? QPS, typical and peak, prompt sizes?
[00:40] Priya Rao: Sure — baseline is ~6 QPS for interactive chat, peaks up to 60 QPS for certain marketing campaigns. Typical prompt length 150-300 tokens; we have a small percentage (maybe 5%) of long contexts up to 4k tokens for recall. For batch embeddings — roughly 200k records nightly, we do them in windows but they need to finish within a 2 hour window.
[01:05] Mark Liu: From infra: tight on budget but we need predictable tail latencies. We're worried about p99 spikes when cluster is noisy.
[01:12] Luis Ortega: Understood. Let's normalize terminology before targets: Redwood uses TTFT — time to first token — and TPOT — time per output token (sometimes called throughput per token). TTFT captures initial latency that matter for perceived responsiveness, TPOT captures streaming/generation speed.
[01:30] Priya Rao: Okay, that matches our intuitive split. For chat UX we care more about TTFT at p95 and p99; for long responses we also need TPOT to be within bounds so streaming doesn't feel sluggish.
[01:42] Maya Chen: Good. Any existing baselines you measure today? Client-side traces?
[01:46] Priya Rao: We have application logs with request->first-byte times and full response times, but they're noisy — some client retries and mobile networks add variance. We'll try to provide server-side traces from our current vendor which capture request received -> token emit.
[02:00] Luis Ortega: That helps. For the POC we'll ask for both: production traces to replay request size distributions and synthetic tests to isolate server-side behavior. We'll compare client-observed TTFT vs server-side TTFT. Expect a delta due to network.
[02:12] Sarah Bennett: How do we set targets? Are there Redwood recommendations?
[02:15] Luis Ortega: We typically suggest tiered SLOs by workload class. Example suggestions (ballpark): chat short prompts (<=512 tokens): TTFT p95 < 150ms, p99 < 350ms; TPOT p95 < 18ms/token, p99 < 45ms/token. For long-context or 4k prompts TTFT will shift — maybe p95 < 350ms, p99 < 700ms. For embeddings batch throughput we target throughput (tokens/sec or items/sec) such that nightly window fits — e.g., 200k records in 2 hours with concurrency X.
[02:48] Priya Rao: Those numbers sound optimistic. Our current vendor posts p95 ~220ms for small chats and p99 ~550ms during spikes. If Redwood can hit your lower p95s consistently that's interesting.
[02:59] Maya Chen: Important to caveat: model choice and quantization matter a lot. If you choose a large 70B model, TTFT and TPOT costs go up. For POC we should pin model & quantization profile.
[03:12] Mark Liu: We'll want to test both a cost-optimized medium model and a higher-quality large model to understand tradeoffs.
[03:18] Luis Ortega: Agreed. Our benchmark plan: 1) Replay production traces against pinned model + config; 2) Synthetic microbench for warm vs cold KV cache; 3) Concurrency sweep (1..64 concurrent requests) to find knee; 4) Measure p50/p95/p99 for TTFT and TPOT, plus cost per 1k tokens. We'll provide harness and scripts.
[03:36] Priya Rao: Can we also test prefix / session cache effects? Some of our UXs reuse system prompts.
[03:40] Luis Ortega: Yes — we'll do cache-warm scenarios: cold (empty KV), steady-state warm, and mid-term (after restart). We'll log cache hit rate and include a run with explicit prefix caching enabled.
[03:50] Sarah Bennett: For measurement windows, what sample sizes do you need to make p99 meaningful?
[03:56] Luis Ortega: Good question — p99 needs decent samples. For a stable estimate, we'd aim for tens of thousands of requests; practical POC we can do targeted stress runs to generate p99 samples. We'll run each config for at least 30 minutes at target QPS, and repeat runs to capture variance.
[04:12] Priya Rao: OK. About measurement points: do you report client-observed, server-observed, and infra-level timings (GPU scheduling)?
[04:19] Luis Ortega: We'll capture multiple layers: client RTT + server ingest -> first byte (server TTFT), model kernel timing (time spent in GPU), and end-to-end from load balancer. We'll provide dashboards with breakdowns. Note: instrumentation has small overhead but gives insight into where tail originates.
[04:36] Maya Chen: One common source of p99 is autoscaling actions or node preemption. Mark, any constraints on bursting and preemption in your infra?
[04:43] Mark Liu: We avoid preemptible for production workloads; for POC we can allow mixed nodes but want to note it. Also need to confirm VPC peering rules if we run Redwood-managed Dedicated in our account.
[04:55] Priya Rao: Security: for Dedicated or Private we need SOC2 scope and SSO integration. Maya, can you share Redwood's security artifacts?
[05:02] Maya Chen: Yes I'll share SOC2 summary and the security checklist. That's in the next steps.
[05:07] Priya Rao: Thanks. Back to SLOs — can you propose a matrix we can sign off on? e.g., Chat-Short, Chat-Long, Batch-Embedding with p95/p99 numbers and measurement method.
[05:17] Luis Ortega: I'll propose a matrix. Example cells: Chat-Short (<=512 tokens): TTFT p95 150ms, p99 350ms; TPOT p95 18ms/token, p99 45ms/token; Measurement: server-side replay, 30m steady-state runs with 3 repeats. Chat-Long (>512 tokens): TTFT p95 350ms, p99 700ms; TPOT p95 22ms/token, p99 60ms/token. Batch-Embedding: throughput target 28k items/hr (to meet 200k in 8 hours) or scale to 100k/hr for 2-hr window; report items/sec and end-to-end job completion median and p99.
[05:52] Sarah Bennett: The embedding numbers need to map to actual VM/GPU counts and cost. Can Redwood show estimated cost delta per throughput tier?
[05:59] Maya Chen: Yes, Redwood Optimize will provide cost estimates given batching/quantization settings. We'll include cost per 1M tokens or per 100k embeddings under each config.
[06:08] Priya Rao: What's the expected timeline for the POC? We need to show results to execs in three weeks.
[06:13] Luis Ortega: For a minimal meaningful POC: week 1 collect traces & finalize config, week 2 run Redwood-managed benchmarks + synth, week 3 analyze and present results. That maps to ~3 weeks. If you want deeper resilience runs add 1 week.
[06:27] Mark Liu: That timeline works. We'll aim to get traces in 48 hours.
[06:30] Priya Rao: Note: our production traffic has diurnal patterns that cause queueing at 17:00 UTC — you might see weird tails if you don't mimic that.
[06:38] Luis Ortega: We'll ask you to label time-of-day peaks; we'll run stress tests including a peak traffic window.
[06:43] Maya Chen: A quick note about metrics: we'll compute p95/p99 across the full window and also within per-minute sliding windows to detect spikes. Also we'll include latency heatmaps by request size.
[06:55] Priya Rao: Good. A few clarifying questions: 1) Does Redwood's benchmark harness emulate auth and headers we use? 2) How do you handle model fallbacks during overload?
[07:03] Luis Ortega: 1) Yes, the harness can inject headers and token bounds; we'll need a safe test key. 2) For overload we can configure automatic fallback to a cheaper model or a degraded config; as part of the POC we can test canary fallback policy so you see graceful degradation.
[07:16] Sarah Bennett: For acceptance criteria, can we propose pass/fail rules? e.g., primary: chat-short TTFT p95 below threshold in 3/4 runs and p99 below threshold in 2/3 runs; otherwise remediation.
[07:27] Luis Ortega: That's reasonable. We typically define: success if p95 target met in 3 consecutive runs and p99 under target in at least 2 runs, and cost per request within X% of budget. We'll draft exact acceptance criteria in the POC doc.
[07:42] Mark Liu: Also include failure modes — e.g., if p99 tail driven by disk IO or network not model, then we mark as non-Redwood.
[07:50] Maya Chen: Good call, we'll include root-cause classification steps.
[07:54] Priya Rao: Anything else on measurement technique? Sometimes p99 is dominated by a few misrouted requests; how do you filter?
[08:00] Luis Ortega: We'll filter client retries and known outliers based on request metadata, but we'll keep raw traces for audit. We'll also run controlled experiments that isolate variables.
[08:09] Maya Chen: I'll summarize deliverables: 1) Redwood sends benchmark harness + RD-POC template + security artifacts; 2) DataWave provides traces and peaks annotated; 3) Redwood runs benchmarks and returns dashboards + cost matrix; 4) Joint review and acceptance decision.
[08:25] Priya Rao: Sounds good. Please note we need redwood to confirm whether the observed client-server delta (e.g., network) will be significant in our numbers.
[08:33] Luis Ortega: We'll provide both server-only and end-to-end numbers and annotate network deltas.
[08:36] Sarah Bennett: On the exec side, we prefer p95 guarantees more than p99 — p99 is nice-to-have but we need predictable p95 to retain users.
[08:46] Maya Chen: Noted. We'll emphasize p95 in the summary and include p99 as tail analysis.
[08:51] Mark Liu: Last operational note: if we go Dedicated, we need to understand autoscale boundaries and burst policy in case of sudden campaign spikes.
[08:59] Luis Ortega: We'll include recommended autoscale policies and burst buffers in the config.
[09:03] Priya Rao: Alright, I'll send traces and a sample of our embedding job config.
[09:07] Maya Chen: Great, thanks Priya. We'll aim to have the harness and RD-POC doc in your inbox by Thursday (2025-03-13).
[09:12] Luis Ortega: I'll propose benchmark windows for the week of 2025-03-17 after we get traces.
[09:18] Sarah Bennett: Thanks everyone.
[09:20] Maya Chen: Quick recap of next steps... (recap).
[09:28] Priya Rao: Thanks — talk soon.
[09:30] [call ends]
